clue.text: Leading edge of Channel unfortunately swamping one French port

indicators.note: the leading edge of a word is its first letter, so take the start of Channel
one piece swamps, or engulfs, the other, so it goes round it

parts.note: alas is an exclamation meaning unfortunately
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Bad luck strikes a French harbour as the Channel's edge floods it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swamping' puts I inside ALAS, and the Channel's leading edge, C, goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Calais is the ferry harbour on the north coast of France facing Dover.

clue.text: Cold infiltrating lorry in icy area

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside, so the first piece goes into the lorry

parts.note: an artic is an articulated lorry, a big British truck with a hinged trailer
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A chill gets into a truck driving through frozen country.
explanation.walkthrough: An ARTIC is British slang for an articulated lorry (a big truck); 'infiltrating' puts C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic is the frozen region around the North Pole, an icy area by any measure.

clue.text: King's Bench offering lofty view of capital

parts.note: King Arthur is the legendary British king, so a king's could be Arthur's
a bench is a seat

explanation.surface: A royal law court is said to offer a high vantage point over the city.
explanation.walkthrough: King's Bench sounds like the old English law court; here it is a king's (Arthur's) seat. ARTHUR'S SEAT is the hill overlooking Edinburgh, Scotland's capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur's Seat is a high hill in Edinburgh whose summit gives sweeping views over the Scottish capital.

clue.text: It's a corny funny book parodying Romans

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd or peculiar, so these letters are arranged oddly

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a satire of ancient Rome as a book of tired jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funny' rearranges the letters of IT'S A CORNY. The Satyricon is Petronius's comic Latin novel mocking Roman society.
explanation.definitionFit: Petronius wrote this satirical Latin novel lampooning the vulgar excesses of Roman life under Nero.

clue.text: Led back, conscious, in a state

indicators.note: back means the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
to be conscious of something is to be aware of it

explanation.surface: Someone guided home, fully alert, but in a bit of a state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LED into DEL; 'in a state' reads as being flustered, but the definition is just 'a state' of the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Delaware is one of the fifty United States, the first to ratify the Constitution.

clue.text: State education's first two elements taken up by Cambridge college

indicators.note: in a down answer taken up means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: the first two letters of the word education
Clare is one of the colleges of Cambridge University

explanation.surface: A Cambridge college adopts the basics of education as a matter of public record.
explanation.walkthrough: Elements suggests chemistry, but here it means letters. In a down entry 'taken up' turns the pair upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To state something is to declare it, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Playful girl comes into endless fortune

indicators.note: one piece entering another goes inside it
endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: luck is fortune
Di is a short girl's name, from Diana

explanation.surface: A young woman inherits a never-ending fortune and feels frisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Di is a common short form of Diana.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludic is a formal word for playful, from Latin ludus, play or game.

clue.text: All of us will take to heart love and sorrow

indicators.note: taking something to heart puts it in the middle of the other piece

parts.note: we means all of us
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: We will all cherish both affection and grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will take to heart' puts O inside WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Woe is deep grief or misery, a literary word for sorrow.

clue.text: Scope to limit competent criticism

indicators.note: to limit something is to set bounds around it, so the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: scope and reach both mean range or extent
a pro, a professional, is competent at the job

explanation.surface: A skilled reviewer's critique is kept within narrow bounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Competent is an adjective here, standing for the noun pro in the sense of an expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A reproach is an expression of disapproval or rebuke, which is criticism.

clue.text: Ecstasy and cocaine, for starters — still high!

indicators.note: starters are the first letters, here of ecstasy and cocaine

parts.note: still and static both mean not moving

explanation.surface: Drugs taken first leave someone motionless and very high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for starters' takes E and C from Ecstasy and cocaine; 'still high' looks like 'still on drugs' but still is STATIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstatic means in a state of rapture, which is being high on happiness.

clue.text: Finish university course in French town

parts.note: to die is to finish or come to an end
PPE is Philosophy, Politics and Economics, a well-known Oxford degree course

explanation.surface: A student completes a degree somewhere in France.
explanation.walkthrough: PPE is Philosophy, Politics and Economics, a famous Oxford degree course.
explanation.definitionFit: Dieppe is a Channel port town in Normandy, northern France.

clue.text: Ice removed from sweet drink

indicators.note: removed from means the first piece is taken out of the second

parts.note: liquorice is a sweet, British for a candy, made from a black root extract
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone takes the ice out of a sugary drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice removed from sweet drink' reads as a cocktail; the sweet is LIQUORICE (a British candy), and taking ICE out of it leaves the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquor is alcoholic drink, especially spirits.

clue.text: Wicked courtesan, non-U, identified as forebear

indicators.note: wicked suggests something bent or twisted, so these letters are rearranged
non- means without, so the letter U is dropped

explanation.surface: A wicked courtesan of low class turns out to be someone's ancestor.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is the old British label for not upper class. Removing U leaves CORTESAN, and 'Wicked' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancestor is someone from whom you are descended, a forebear.

clue.text: Quiet time for news, as one's implied?

indicators.note: implied says the clue words are what the answer would produce if read as an instruction

parts.note: these words are what the answer's wordplay produces: silly, an anagram signal, works on the second word to give them

explanation.surface: A newspaper's slow summer stretch, as someone hinted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'implied' says the answer read as wordplay gives AS ONE'S: 'silly' is an anagram signal applied to SEASON. The silly season is the summer lull when papers print trivia.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalists call the summer lull, when Parliament is away and trivial stories fill papers, by this name.

clue.text: Coppers not in general circulation?

parts.note: coppers as both coins and police officers: ones kept out of public sight are covert agents of the state

explanation.surface: Some pennies are being withheld from use.
explanation.walkthrough: Coppers suggests small coins out of circulation; it means police officers whose work is hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret police force operates covertly, not known to the general public.

clue.text: Deep moves to keep eager university teacher

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece encloses the others
moves means the letters are shifted about

parts.note: agog means eager and excited

explanation.surface: An excited don is drawn to profound thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moves' rearranges DEEP into PEDE, which then holds the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedagogue is a teacher, often a strict or pedantic one.

clue.text: Dog and another pet seizing old item of 'clothing

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them, as to tail them

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold of, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: a cat is a pet, as well as the dog

explanation.surface: A dog and a cat fight over an old garment.
explanation.walkthrough: Dog looks like an animal but is the verb, to follow; the stray apostrophe before clothing is a printing mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailcoat is a formal jacket cut short at the front with long tails behind.

clue.text: Passed on hint: a dye mixes eventually

parts.note: someone who has passed on, died, is the late

indicators.note: mixes means the letters are stirred together into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone passes on a tip for blending a dye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixes' rearranges HINT A DYE into IN THE DAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Late in the day is an idiom for at a late stage, finally, so eventually.

clue.text: An end to life when given to man, note well

definitions.text: An end to life when given to man, note well

indicators.note: given to means added after the other pieces

parts.note: he is a man in pronoun form
NB stands for nota bene, Latin for note well
taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, here of life

explanation.surface: A warning that this brings death if given to a person.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay: 'when given to' adds AN and the last letter of life to HE + NB. Henbane is a poisonous plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Henbane is a highly poisonous nightshade plant whose dose can kill a human.

clue.text: Space initially curtailed for horse in small ornamental circle

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter
curtailed means having its tail, the last letter, cut off

parts.note: equine means of a horse, so it stands in for it

explanation.surface: A small spangle is fixed to a cut-down horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curtailed' cuts the final E off EQUINE; S from Space's initial goes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A sequin is a small shiny disc sewn onto clothing for decoration.

clue.text: Untidy female bird on piece of wood

indicators.note: on means placed after the other piece in an across answer

parts.note: a slat is a thin strip of wood
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A scruffy woman spots a bird perched on a plank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts the bird after the plank in an across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A slattern is an old, derogatory word for a dirty, untidy woman.

clue.text: Former skill shown up as surplus

parts.note: ex means former

indicators.note: shown up in a down answer means read upwards, backwards

parts.note: art is skill

explanation.surface: An old talent is exposed as being unnecessary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shown up' turns ART into TRA, written upwards in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means more than needed, which is a surplus.

clue.text: Good to dance clutching waist of natty German girl

indicators.note: clutching means holding inside

parts.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance

indicators.note: the waist of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A girl from Germany dances well, holding a smart partner by the waist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clutching' puts T, the waist of natty, inside REEL. Gretel is the girl of Hansel and Gretel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gretel is a German girl's name, the sister in the Grimm tale of Hansel and Gretel.

clue.text: Fellow, posh chap, returned this neat quip.

indicators.note: returned means read backwards, turning the whole pair

parts.note: Tom is a man's name, a fellow
a nob is an upper-class person in British slang

explanation.surface: A man and a toff come back with a clever remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reverses TOMNOB as a whole. Bon mot is French for a witty remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A bon mot, French for good word, is a clever witty remark.

clue.text: Lots of people? Not entirely —— just one

indicators.note: not entirely means one letter, the last, is missing

parts.note: many means lots of people, as in many believe

explanation.surface: Is it a crowd? Not quite: only a single person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' drops the last letter of MANY.
explanation.definitionFit: A man is a single person, so just one individual rather than many.

clue.text: John, say —. American following Gold Rush?

indicators.note: following means placed after the other pieces

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a gust is a sudden rush of wind

explanation.surface: An American arrives after the Gold Rush.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank is a first name: Augustus John was a Welsh painter. The Gold Rush picture hides the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustus John was a celebrated Welsh portrait painter, so this name fills the blank before John.

clue.text: Attitude evident in wise man before copper came in.

indicators.note: evident in means seen inside the other piece

parts.note: a sage is a wise man
tone is attitude, as in the tone of a letter

explanation.surface: A wise man shows a certain attitude before the police arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper looks like the police; it is the metal whose arrival ended the Stone Age.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stone Age was the prehistoric period before metal, starting with copper, came into use.

clue.text: Cause of weather change broadcast online

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: News of a shift in climate goes out on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges ONLINE.
explanation.definitionFit: El Niño is the Pacific warming event that disrupts global weather patterns.
